question: Europe’s population is ageing dramatically. The need for quality healthcare and long-term care services is increasing at the same rhythm. The Member States and the EU as a whole need to start looking for answers to the problem before it reaches a critical phase. The EU is already experiencing a critical shortage of healthcare personnel such as nurses.

This shortage will only become worse during the years to come and has the potential to endanger the EU’s crisis resilience and security of supply. At the same time, many other phenomena, such as the advance of climate change, will only increase, rather than reduce, the need for care.

This challenge can only be resolved together at the European level with actions related to working conditions, pay and quality of training of care personnel. Parliament has already drawn attention to this issue in its resolution on European care in 20221.
Does the Commission intend to create a common European strategy to combat the shortage of healthcare and long-term care staff and guarantee the availability of healthcare labour in Europe?
Resolution of 5 July 2022 towards a common European action on care. https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/TA-9-2022-0278_EN.html.
answer: The Commission acknowledges that the health workforce faces challenges related to working conditions and labour shortages. This requires appropriate measures in line with the share of competences between Member States and the EU.

According to Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, Member States are responsible for the management of health services, which includes allocation of resources to ensure sufficient availability of health workforce.
The Commission supports Member States in strengthening the health workforce through several targeted initiatives, funded by EU4Health, Erasmus+ and the Third Health Programme.

For instance, a Joint Action on forecasting and planning of health workforce (2); five projects focusing on workforce retention, task shifting and medical deserts (3); actions on skills development under the BeWell project (4), seven projects developing training programmes and focusing on digital skills (5), and a new action addressing shortages of nurses (6).
Other EU funding instruments such as the Cohesion Policy Funds and the Recovery and Resilience Facility can support complementary actions.

The 2022 European Care Strategy (7) and Council Recommendation on access to high-quality affordable long-term care (8) aim at improving the situation of long-term care workforce to increase the sector’s attractiveness, against the broader background of the recent action plan to tackle labour and skills shortages (9).
